# Wedding Planner Platform - Complete Project Documentation ## 🎯 Project Overview A full-stack wedding planning marketplace connecting couples with wedding vendors. The platform allows vendors to showcase their services, couples to browse and book vendors, and admins to moderate content. ## 🏗️ Architecture ### Tech Stack - **Frontend**: React 19, React Router, Vite, TailwindCSS, Bootstrap 5 - **Backend**: Node.js, Express 5, MongoDB, Mongoose - **Authentication**: JWT (JSON Web Tokens), bcryptjs - **File Upload**: Cloudinary, Multer - **State Management**: React Hooks (useState, useEffect) ### Project Structure 
wedding-planner/
├── backend/
│   ├── config/          # Cloudinary configuration
│   ├── controllers/     # Business logic (auth, vendor, admin)
│   ├── middlewares/     # Auth & validation middleware
│   ├── models/          # MongoDB schemas (User, Vendor)
│   ├── routes/          # API endpoints
│   └── app.js           # Express server setup
│
└── frontend/
    └── src/
        ├── components/  # Reusable components (Navbar, Footer, etc.)
        ├── pages/       # Main pages (Login, SignUp, AdminDashboard)
        └── vendorpages/ # Vendor-specific pages
## 👥 User Roles & Features ### 1. Couple/User Role - Browse wedding vendors by category and city - View vendor details, photos, videos - Submit inquiries (check-ins) to vendors - Leave reviews and ratings - Create account and login ### 2. Vendor Role - Create vendor profile with business details - Add vendor posts with images/videos - Manage media gallery - View and respond to leads (check-ins) - Track profile views and analytics - Edit vendor information - Requires admin approval before going live ### 3. Admin Role - View platform statistics (users, vendors, approvals) - Approve/reject vendor submissions - Add approval notes - View all users - Monitor platform activity - Full moderation control ## 🔐 Authentication System ### Registration Flow 1. User signs up with name, email, password, role (couple/vendor) 2. Password is hashed with bcrypt (10 salt rounds) 3. User data stored in MongoDB 4. Redirect to login page ### Login Flow 1. User enters email and password 2. Backend validates credentials 3. JWT token generated (24h expiry) 4. Token + user data stored in localStorage 5. Role-based redirect (admin → admin dashboard, vendor → vendor hub, couple → home) ### Protected Routes - ProtectedRoute: Requires authentication - AdminRoute: Requires admin role - Token sent in Authorization header for API calls ## 📊 Database Models ### User Model 
{
  name: String (required),
  email: String (required, unique),
  password: String (required, hashed),
  role: String (couple/vendor/admin),
  vendorProfile: {
    businessName: String,
    category: String,
    city: String,
    phone: String,
    about: String,
    profileImage: String,
    completed: Boolean
  },
  vendor: [ObjectId] // References to Vendor posts
}
### Vendor Model 
{
  businessname: String (required),
  description: String (required),
  image1: String (required),
  image2, image3: String,
  galleryImages: [String],
  galleryVideos: [String],
  media: [{ url, type }],
  price: Number (required),
  phone: String (required),
  city: String (required),
  state: String,
  landMark: String,
  category: String (required),
  user: ObjectId (required),
  approvalStatus: String (pending/approved/rejected),
  approvalNote: String,
  approvedAt: Date,
  approvedBy: ObjectId,
  rating: Number (0-5),
  viewsCount: Number,
  viewLogs: [{ viewerName, viewerEmail, viewerPhone, viewedAt }],
  reviews: [{ name, rating, comment, createdAt }],
  checkIns: [{ name, email, phone, eventDate, guests, message, status, createdAt }],
  isBooked: Boolean
}
## 🛣️ API Endpoints ### Authentication Routes (/auth) - POST /auth/signup - Register new user - POST /auth/login - Login user - POST /auth/vendor-onboarding - Complete vendor profile (protected) ### Vendor Routes (/vendor/post) - GET /vendor/post - Get all approved vendors - GET /vendor/post/:id - Get single vendor - POST /vendor/post - Create vendor post (protected) - PUT /vendor/post/:id - Update vendor post (protected) - DELETE /vendor/post/:id - Delete vendor post (protected) - POST /vendor/post/:id/checkin - Submit inquiry - POST /vendor/post/:id/review - Add review - GET /vendor/post/user/:userId - Get user's vendors ### Admin Routes (/admin) - GET /admin/dashboard - Get platform stats (protected, admin only) - GET /admin/vendors?status=pending - Get vendors by status (protected, admin only) - GET /admin/users - Get all users (protected, admin only) - PATCH /admin/vendors/:id/approval - Approve/reject vendor (protected, admin only) ## 🎨 Frontend Pages ### Public Pages - / - Home page with hero, popular venues, categories - /vendor - Vendor listing page - /vendor/explore - Vendor hub/explore page - /vendorpost/:id - Vendor detail page ### Auth Pages - /login - Login page - /signup - Signup page with role selection ### Protected Pages (Require Login) - /vendor/join - Vendor onboarding form - /vendor/admin - Vendor dashboard - /vendor/admin/:id/leads - Vendor leads management - /vendor/admin/:id/media - Vendor media manager - /vendors/wedding-venues/addpost - Add new vendor post - /vendorpost/edit/:id - Edit vendor post ### Admin Pages (Require Admin Role) - /admin - Admin dashboard with moderation queue ## 🔧 Key Features Implementation ### 1. Reviews & Ratings - Couples leave reviews after viewing vendor - 1-5 star rating system - Average rating calculated and displayed - Reviews shown on vendor detail page ### 5. Analytics - View count tracking - Viewer information logged - Lead conversion tracking - Admin sees platform-wide stats ## 🚀 Getting Started ### Backend Setup

Your idea can become a real business in India, but it should be built as a trust-first wedding marketplace, not just a vendor listing site. The India wedding services market was valued at USD 103.93 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach USD 228.69 billion by 2030, so the category is large enough for a serious platform if you solve trust, discovery, and bookings well. Grand View Research

For India, I would shape the platform like this: couples should be able to search, compare, chat, request quotes, book, and pay advances; vendors should be able to create verified profiles, manage packages, respond to leads, show gallery/media, and track inquiries; admins should be able to verify vendors, approve listings, control fraud, and handle disputes. The biggest Indian-market advantages will be WhatsApp-first communication, local-city search, package pricing in INR, Hindi/regional language support, and vendor verification badges.

For compliance, build it properly from day one. Because you will collect names, phone numbers, event dates, photos, and payments, your product should follow the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; the Act is the current Indian law for digital personal data, and its consent standard requires consent to be free, specific, informed, unconditional, and unambiguous. India Code+1 Since this is an online marketplace, the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 also matter, so you should keep pricing transparent, display grievance/contact details, and support complaint handling clearly. Consumer Affairs+2 If your turnover grows, GST becomes relevant too; CBIC’s FAQ says service suppliers are liable to register when aggregate turnover exceeds ₹20 lakh (with some state exceptions). CBIC GST

To make it industry-level, build in phases:

Phase 1 — MVP to launch

  • Vendor signup, login, and profile verification
  • Vendor category + city filters
  • Vendor detail pages with photos, videos, price, packages, reviews
  • Inquiry/check-in form
  • Admin approval dashboard
  • Basic analytics: views, leads, conversion

Phase 2 — Real business features

  • Booking calendar and date availability
  • Advance payment / booking token
  • Vendor subscription plans
  • Featured listing / promoted placement
  • Contract, invoice, refund, cancellation flow
  • WhatsApp and email notifications

Phase 3 — India scale

  • Multi-city expansion
  • Hindi + regional language UI
  • SEO landing pages for each city/category
  • Vendor onboarding team for offline acquisition
  • Fraud detection and duplicate listing checks
  • Customer support and dispute resolution workflow

Your monetization model can be:

  • Vendor subscription plans
  • Featured / sponsored listings
  • Lead fees
  • Booking commission
  • Premium tools for vendors like CRM, lead tracking, and media analytics

A strong one-line positioning statement for your project is:

“A verified wedding marketplace for India that helps couples find trusted vendors and helps vendors get qualified leads and bookings.”

MASTER DEVELOPMENT PROMPT: BUILD A PREMIUM INDIAN WEDDING MARKETPLACE

1. Your Role

Act as a senior full-stack engineer, premium UI/UX designer, product architect, Indian wedding industry expert, and SaaS marketplace consultant.

I have an existing full-stack project called Wedding Planner, built to connect couples with wedding vendors across India.

Your task is to transform my existing project into a production-quality, responsive, beautiful, fully functional Indian wedding marketplace that I can deploy publicly and develop into a real business.

Do not create just a static landing page, a Figma-style mockup, or a collection of attractive cards. Implement the actual application using my existing codebase, connect the frontend to the backend, and ensure that the important buttons, forms, searches, dashboards, authentication, and vendor workflows work correctly.

First inspect the complete repository, understand the existing functionality and API contracts, and then implement the solution without unnecessarily rebuilding working features.

2. Existing Technology Stack

Frontend

  • React 19

  • Vite

  • React Router

  • Tailwind CSS

  • Bootstrap 5

  • Axios

  • React Hooks

  • React Icons / Lucide icons where appropriate

Backend

  • Node.js

  • Express 5

  • MongoDB

  • Mongoose

  • JWT authentication

  • bcryptjs

  • Multer

  • Cloudinary

  • Joi validation

Existing Project Structure

wedding-planner/
├── backend/
│   ├── config/
│   ├── controllers/
│   ├── middlewares/
│   ├── models/
│   ├── routes/
│   └── app.js
└── frontend/
    └── src/
        ├── components/
        ├── pages/
        └── vendorpages/

Preserve the current architecture wherever practical. Inspect the actual repository before changing files. Reuse existing components, routes, models, and API endpoints where possible.

Do not replace functioning backend features with hardcoded frontend data.

3. Product Vision

Create an elegant Indian wedding discovery and planning platform that helps couples:

  • Discover trusted wedding vendors.

  • Search by city, category, wedding budget, and wedding style.

  • Explore different Indian wedding traditions.

  • View realistic vendor portfolios, packages, prices, and reviews.

  • Send inquiries and request quotations.

  • Check availability and eventually book services.

  • Save their favourite vendors and plan their wedding.

  • Communicate with vendors and track inquiry status.

Vendors should be able to create business profiles, upload portfolios, manage pricing and leads, and convert inquiries into customers.

Administrators should control verification, approvals, reports, moderation, disputes, and platform activity.

Brand positioning:

“Every Tradition. Every Love Story. One Beautiful Beginning.”

The brand should feel premium but accessible to Indian middle-class and affluent families alike.

Do not copy the exact design of WedMeGood, WeddingWire, or other competitors. Use established marketplace usability principles while developing an original visual identity.

4. Creative Visual Design Direction

Brand personality

The visual identity should feel:

  • Luxurious and editorial.

  • Indian and culturally authentic.

  • Romantic without being overly decorative.

  • Premium without being intimidating.

  • Modern, minimal, and easy to navigate.

  • Trustworthy enough for couples spending substantial amounts on a wedding.

Avoid generic templates dominated by bright pink gradients, excessive rounded cards, floating icons, cartoon illustrations, and repetitive sections.

Use authentic wedding photography, elegant typography, excellent spacing, subtle animations, and a consistent design system.

Colour palette

Use a sophisticated Indian wedding-inspired palette:

:root {
  --color-primary: #762B3F;
  --color-primary-dark: #501A2B;
  --color-secondary: #D9A441;
  --color-marigold: #E99B35;
  --color-ivory: #FFF9F0;
  --color-background: #FAF7F2;
  --color-surface: #FFFFFF;
  --color-text: #27211F;
  --color-muted: #746B67;
  --color-border: #EAE1D8;
  --color-success: #26734D;
  --color-error: #B42332;
}

Use burgundy and deep wine for the primary brand identity, antique gold for restrained highlights, and ivory for warmth.

Use regional wedding colours in actual photography and selected campaign sections. Do not force every component to use gradients.

Typography

Choose elegant and readable fonts:

  • Headings: Playfair Display or a comparable editorial serif.

  • Body: Inter, Manrope, or another modern sans-serif.

  • Prices, forms, navigation, and dashboard data: a highly readable sans-serif.

Use locally available fonts or reliable web-font fallbacks. Avoid loading excessive font files.

Photography and decorative details

Use authentic, high-quality images depicting Indian weddings:

  • Realistic bridal portraits and couples.

  • Decorated mandaps and wedding stages.

  • Floral arrangements, marigold garlands, and traditional torans.

  • Mehendi ceremonies and haldi celebrations.

  • Palace weddings and destination weddings.

  • Intimate home weddings and contemporary celebrations.

  • Regional clothing, rituals, food, venues, and jewellery.

Use restrained decorative references such as alpana, rangoli, kolam, floral patterns, brass lamps, and architectural arches where culturally appropriate.

Do not mix religious symbols or rituals randomly just to make a design look Indian.

Use licensed or properly usable images. Include image loading states, meaningful alternative text, suitable crops, and graceful fallbacks if images fail to load.

5. Complete Homepage Design

Implement every homepage section as a reusable React component.

Section 1: Premium Navigation

Create a sophisticated navigation bar with:

Left:

  • Original brand logo, such as a refined floral emblem combined with a wedding-inspired wordmark.

  • Brand name: “WedAura” as a provisional name, configurable later.

Centre or right:

  • Find Vendors.

  • Wedding Venues.

  • Photographers.

  • Bridal Makeup.

  • Decor & Planning.

  • Wedding Ideas.

  • Real Weddings.

Far right:

  • Search icon.

  • Wishlist.

  • Log In.

  • “Join as Vendor” CTA.

Requirements:

  • Sticky navigation on scroll.

  • Responsive hamburger menu.

  • Accessible dropdowns.

  • Active navigation states.

  • Functional routing.

  • User account menu after login.

  • Vendor dashboard shortcut for authenticated vendors.

  • No overlapping elements on mobile.

Create a subtle announcement strip for promotions or useful wedding-planning content, configurable from the application rather than permanently hardcoded.

Section 2: Cinematic Wedding Hero

Create a premium, full-width hero featuring a beautiful, authentic Indian wedding photograph.

The image should occupy most of the visual space and have a carefully designed overlay so that the text is readable.

Example content:

Eyebrow:
“YOUR STORY. YOUR TRADITIONS. YOUR PERFECT DAY.”

Main heading:
“Find Everything Your Wedding Deserves.”

Supporting copy:
“Discover trusted wedding professionals, beautiful venues, and thoughtful inspiration to bring your celebration to life.”

Add a functional search panel with:

  1. City or wedding destination.

  2. Vendor category.

  3. Wedding date, where applicable.

  4. Budget range, where applicable.

  5. Search button.

Below the search panel, show quick-search suggestions such as:

Popular destinations:
Delhi, Mumbai, Jaipur, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Lucknow, Udaipur, Goa, Siliguri.

Popular categories:
Photographers, Wedding Venues, Bridal Makeup, Decorators, Caterers.

Do not make every field mandatory. Keep search straightforward.

On mobile, display a simplified heading and a well-designed expandable search form.

The search must connect to the existing vendor API and preserve search filters using URL query parameters wherever practical.

Section 3: Trust and Service Highlights

Create an elegant horizontal trust strip with concise messages such as:

  • Verified vendor profiles.

  • Transparent pricing where available.

  • Real portfolios.

  • Direct inquiries.

  • Wedding planning across India.

Use restrained icons and concise labels.

Do not claim that every vendor is verified, every price is guaranteed, or every booking is protected unless those features are actually implemented and operational.

Any displayed platform statistics must come from the backend. Do not invent numbers such as 10,000 couples or 5,000 vendors.

Section 4: Explore by Wedding Tradition

Make cultural discovery one of the platform's most distinctive features.

Heading:
“Celebrate the Wedding That Is Uniquely Yours.”

Supporting text:
“Discover professionals who understand your traditions, rituals, preferences, and celebration style.”

Build a visually rich collection of wedding tradition cards or an image-led horizontal carousel.

Include examples such as:

  • Bengali Weddings.

  • Punjabi and Sikh Weddings.

  • Tamil Weddings.

  • Telugu Weddings.

  • Gujarati Weddings.

  • Marathi Weddings.

  • Rajasthani and Marwari Weddings.

  • Malayali Weddings.

  • Assamese Weddings.

  • Kashmiri Weddings.

  • Muslim Weddings and Nikah Celebrations.

  • Christian Weddings.

  • Buddhist Weddings.

  • Jain Weddings.

  • Tribal and Indigenous Wedding Traditions.

  • Interfaith Weddings.

  • Civil and Court Weddings.

These are cultural discovery options, not a definitive classification of all Indian communities. Regional traditions overlap, and individuals may follow different combinations of customs.

Do not treat caste as a mandatory profile field or use caste to restrict access to vendors. Allow users to describe their cultural preferences voluntarily, respectfully, and only where relevant.

Each card should feature a relevant photograph, concise description, and “Explore Weddings” link.

Clicking a card should open a real discovery page or a correctly filtered search experience.

Where appropriate, support local-language preferences and regional vendors.

Do not fabricate cultural information. Represent communities accurately, and never make one tradition look superior to another.

Display real vendors retrieved from the backend.

Add category tabs, for example:
All Vendors, Venues, Photography, Makeup, Decor, Catering.

Include a “View All Vendors” link.

Implement skeleton loaders, empty states, image fallbacks, and API error handling.

Never fabricate testimonials, ratings, review counts, vendor credentials, or successful bookings.

  3. Connect — Contact vendors, discuss requirements, and plan bookings.

For vendors:

  3. Receive and manage qualified inquiries.

Create a trust-focused section using editorial cards or a split layout.

  • Clear vendor profiles.

  • Real portfolio evidence.

  • Transparent package information.

  • Secure handling of personal information.

  • Support for inquiry and booking workflows.

Only describe features that actually exist.

6. Build the Complete User Experience

The homepage must not be the only polished page. Apply the same design quality to all primary workflows.

Public Pages

  • Homepage.

  • Vendor directory.

  • Search results.

  • Vendor category pages.

  • Wedding tradition discovery pages.

  • Destination and venue pages.

  • Vendor profile detail page.

  • Inspiration and article pages.

  • About and contact pages.

  • FAQ and help pages.

Authentication Pages

  • Login.

  • Registration.

  • Forgot password.

  • Password reset.

  • Role selection where appropriate.

Use clear validation, loading states, accessible form controls, useful errors, and redirects that preserve intended navigation.

Couple Dashboard

Create an account dashboard with:

  • Profile settings.

  • Saved vendors.

  • Recent searches where practical.

  • Inquiry history.

  • Inquiry status.

  • Wedding preferences.

  • Budget planner.

  • Notifications where implemented.

Do not expose private vendor contact records or other users' data.

Vendor Dashboard

Design a professional dashboard with:

  • Profile completion.

  • Business details.

  • Service categories and service areas.

  • Portfolio and media manager.

  • Packages and pricing.

  • Inquiry management.

  • Inquiry status updates.

  • Profile views and analytics.

  • Approval status.

  • Business settings.

Support practical mobile management because many small vendors will use the platform on their phones.

Admin Dashboard

Build an industry-style administration interface with:

  • Platform metrics from the database.

  • Vendor approval queue.

  • Vendor verification and document review.

  • Approve and reject actions.

  • Approval notes.

  • User management.

  • Reports and moderation.

  • Inquiry or complaint review where supported.

  • Audit history for important administrative actions.

Verify admin permissions on the backend. Hiding an admin page on the frontend is not sufficient security.

7. Vendor Search and Filtering

Implement real search across available vendor data.

Search inputs should support:

  • City.

  • State.

  • Category.

  • Budget range.

  • Minimum rating where ratings exist.

  • Cultural or service preferences where vendors explicitly provide them.

  • Wedding date availability only when an availability feature exists.

Requirements:

  • Combine multiple filters correctly.

  • Add sorting by relevance, price, and rating where supported.

  • Implement pagination.

  • Use URL query parameters so links can be shared.

  • Provide clear filters and reset functionality.

  • Show result counts based on actual data.

  • Add useful empty states.

  • Debounce text search where appropriate.

  • Validate all inputs on the backend.

  • Do not filter vendors based on protected characteristics or assume a vendor belongs to a cultural community based on their name or appearance.

8. Backend and Database Integration

Inspect and improve the existing Mongoose models without breaking existing functionality.

Review:

  • User.

  • Vendor.

  • Reviews.

  • Inquiries/check-ins.

  • Approval records.

  • Vendor media.

  • Availability.

  • Bookings, if implemented.

  • Saved vendors, if implemented.

  • Notifications, if implemented.

Create additional models only when required by a feature.

Use consistent field naming, schema validation, indexes, timestamps, suitable references, and pagination.

Critical backend requirements:

  • All sensitive changes require authorization.

  • Users can modify only their own profiles and resources unless explicitly authorized.

  • Vendors can modify only their own listings.

  • Only admins can approve or reject listings.

  • Only approved, published vendors are publicly visible.

  • Private contact information and internal moderation notes are protected.

  • Reviews and ratings must be validated and calculated consistently.

  • Uploaded files must be validated by size and allowed type.

  • API responses should have a consistent structure.

  • Errors must be logged appropriately without leaking secrets.

  • MongoDB queries must avoid unsafe assumptions about IDs and user ownership.

Use the actual project configuration and endpoints after inspecting them. Do not assume the supplied documentation perfectly matches the current code.

9. Industry-Level Authentication and Security

Audit the existing JWT and bcrypt implementation.

Implement or improve:

  • Secure password hashing.

  • Login and registration validation.

  • Role-based authorization.

  • Token expiration handling.

  • Safe logout and session handling.

  • Rate limiting for sensitive endpoints.

  • Appropriate CORS configuration.

  • Helmet or equivalent security headers.

  • Request payload limits.

  • Secure file-upload validation.

  • Environment variable validation.

  • Protection against mass assignment.

  • Appropriate error handling.

  • Server-side authorization on every protected operation.

Review how JWTs are stored and transported. Prefer secure, HttpOnly cookies where the authentication architecture supports them; configure CSRF protection and cookie security appropriately if using cookies. If retaining bearer tokens, minimize exposure and do not store secrets in frontend code.

Never commit API keys, production database credentials, JWT secrets, or Cloudinary secrets.

Add production privacy and consent flows suitable for Indian users, and have the final privacy policy and legal terms reviewed for the actual business operations.

10. Performance, SEO, Accessibility, and Reliability

Implement:

  • Responsive image sizing and lazy loading.

  • Route-level code splitting where appropriate.

  • Efficient vendor queries.

  • Pagination rather than unbounded results.

  • Optimized production assets.

  • Skeleton loading states.

  • Network error handling.

  • Accessible semantic HTML.

  • Keyboard-friendly navigation.

  • Visible focus states.

  • Suitable text contrast.

  • Reduced-motion support.

  • Descriptive page titles and metadata.

  • Canonical URLs where appropriate.

  • Open Graph metadata.

  • Productively structured category and vendor URLs.

  • Structured data only when the content qualifies and the values are accurate.

  • Helpful 404 and error pages.

Do not render the same heavy animation on every element. Animation should enhance usability rather than reduce performance.

Test the interface at approximately:

  • 360–390 px mobile widths.

  • 768 px tablet widths.

  • 1024 px laptop widths.

  • 1440 px desktop widths.

11. Technical Implementation Rules

  1. Inspect the complete existing repository before implementation.

  2. Identify the entry points, routes, dependencies, API services, authentication flow, and Tailwind configuration.

  3. Create reusable UI components instead of duplicating markup.

  4. Maintain consistent naming and folder organization.

  5. Use a single, consistent API configuration.

  6. Use environment variables for frontend and backend configuration.

  7. Preserve existing working authentication and vendor workflows.

  8. Avoid unnecessary dependency installation.

  9. Remove dead code and duplicate styles where appropriate.

  10. Make every visible button perform its advertised action.

  11. Never leave a form that silently does nothing.

  12. Do not make up backend responses to simulate success.

  13. Never claim a booking, payment, or newsletter subscription succeeded unless it actually did.

  14. Keep empty states professional when the database contains no records.

  15. Do not silently overwrite working environment files or production data.

  16. Provide database migrations or safe migration instructions if the schema changes.

  17. Maintain a clear separation between public, couple, vendor, and administrative permissions.

Use the existing React Router structure where appropriate. Add new routes only when the corresponding features have real implementations.

12. Testing Requirements

Before considering the work finished:

  • Install or verify required dependencies.

  • Run the frontend production build.

  • Run backend tests and lint checks if configured.

  • Test frontend-to-backend API communication.

  • Test registration and login.

  • Test each role's protected routes.

  • Test public vendor listing and detail pages.

  • Test vendor creation and the pending-approval workflow.

  • Test admin approval and rejection.

  • Test vendor ownership restrictions.

  • Test inquiry submission and vendor lead management.

  • Test invalid inputs and expired or missing authentication.

  • Test mobile navigation and responsive layouts.

  • Verify upload failures and missing images.

  • Verify search filters and pagination.

  • Check browser console errors.

  • Confirm that production build configuration works.

Do not claim that functionality has been tested if it has not actually been executed.

If a required external service is unavailable, document the limitation and provide a working local-development alternative.

13. Deployment and Business Readiness

Prepare the application for deployment using suitable services.

Suggested architecture:

  • Frontend: a suitable React/Vite hosting service or static hosting platform.

  • Backend: a Node.js-compatible application hosting service.

  • Database: MongoDB Atlas.

  • Image hosting: Cloudinary.

  • Domain: a custom domain selected after a brand-name and trademark review.

Configure:

  • Production frontend URL.

  • Production API URL.

  • MongoDB connection string.

  • JWT secret.

  • Cloudinary credentials.

  • CORS allowed origins.

  • Health-check endpoint.

  • Production startup command.

  • Environment variable documentation.

  • Logging and error reporting.

  • Database backups and recovery planning.

  • DNS and HTTPS instructions.

Document how to deploy the frontend and backend independently and how to test the final live application.

Never place backend secrets in Vite variables exposed to the browser.

Before accepting real customer payments, implement the complete payment provider integration, booking state transitions, refund and cancellation workflows, reconciliation, and appropriate verification. Do not simulate payments.

Also document the operational requirements for customer support, vendor onboarding, dispute handling, data retention, privacy requests, and marketplace policies.

14. Final Deliverables

I expect you to produce:

  1. A redesigned premium homepage with all essential sections.

  2. A consistent reusable design system.

  3. A fully responsive navigation and footer.

  4. A functional vendor discovery and detail experience.

  5. Culturally diverse wedding discovery pages.

  6. Properly integrated authentication.

  7. Working couple, vendor, and admin workflows.

  8. API and database improvements where necessary.

  9. Robust validation, access control, and error handling.

  10. A production build and deployment instructions.

  11. An updated README with local setup and environment variables.

  12. A list of all files changed.

  13. A clear list of features actually implemented and tested.

  14. A list of any remaining tasks or blocked integrations.

15. Definition of Done

The project is complete only when:

  • The homepage looks premium, realistic, and distinctly Indian.

  • Cultural and regional wedding traditions are represented respectfully.

  • All visible search and navigation features work.

  • Vendor listings load from the backend.

  • User roles have the correct permissions.

  • Vendor approval works end to end.

  • Forms have validation and useful feedback.

  • Mobile and desktop layouts work properly.

  • The application builds successfully.

  • Deployment instructions match the actual code.

  • There are no fabricated testimonials, invented statistics, fake payment confirmations, or misleading verification badges.

Your First Action

Start by inspecting the repository and its existing implementation. Then create a concise implementation plan, identify the highest-risk issues, and immediately begin modifying the actual source files.

Prioritize the complete homepage and the working discovery-to-inquiry journey first. Continue with the dashboards, security, testing, and deployment readiness.

Do not stop after generating a plan or a design document. Implement the real application in the existing codebase, run the available checks, and report exactly what works and what remains.

My design recommendation for your business

1. Premium homepage

Ivory, deep burgundy, antique gold, editorial typography, and authentic wedding photography. Avoid making every section a pink gradient.

2. Regional wedding discovery

Showcase Bengali, Punjabi, Tamil, Gujarati, Assamese, Sikh, Muslim, Christian, Buddhist, Jain, tribal, interfaith, and other wedding traditions with relevant imagery and services.

3. Real vendor marketplace

Build the actual business around searchable vendor profiles, transparent packages, genuine reviews, enquiries, verification, and eventually real bookings and payments.

One important business decision: design the platform around wedding traditions, regional preferences, and service requirements rather than using caste as a vendor eligibility filter. This lets couples explore culturally relevant wedding services without excluding people or making assumptions about them.
